newsitem.title: UK: British paper says sorry after trial collapses.
newsitem.headline: British paper says sorry after trial collapses.

text.p: The Evening Standard newspaper offered "an unqualified, unconditional apology" on Friday after running a story that caused a British court case to collapse.
Judge Maurice Kay listened intently to the apology and asked the government's top legal adviser to rule if the paper should face contempt of court proceedings.
"I shall refer the matter to the Attorney General with a report and he will have to decide what to do," said Kay, one day after halting the trial because of prejudicial publicity.
He ruled that five Irish Republican Army prisoners and an armed robber -- all charged in connection with an escape from a top security jail -- should not be tried again on the charges.
The men's criminal histories should not have been mentioned by the media during the trial and their legal team had successfully argued that the article prejudiced their trial.
Max Hastings, editor of the London daily, did not speak inside the southeast London courtroom but was said to be "mortified" by the whole matter, which he blamed on human error.
"We are desperately sorry that a piece of carelessness in our office caused the abandonment of these proceedings.
"This is one of those mistakes that happen through human error," Hastings told reporters after the hearing.
The paper's lawyer Kuldip Singh said Hastings was "mortified" that his paper had erred and that it was never the Standard's intention to scupper the court proceedings.
"We accept responsibility where it ought to lie," he told the court. "Human error has led to its happening."
David Eady, representing the Attorney General, told the court contempt was not easily established and that a decision on proceedings would require careful reflection.
It was the second time the men had faced trial on the charges; the original hearing was also halted due to publicity problems.
